terms.name: Sensitivity
terms.location: Mouse Aim, in your Config's aim settings (Hip and ADS). Motion Aim has its own Sensitivity.
terms.summary: How far you move the mouse for one full turn in game, in centimeters. Lower is faster.

definition.text: Mouse sensitivity is in cm/360 or "distance (in centimeters) to perform a full turn". That means, lower values produce faster aiming speeds.

citations.quote: Mouse sensitivity is in cm/360 or "distance (in centimeters) to perform a full turn". That means, lower values produce faster aiming speeds.
Mouse sensitivity is set in centimeters-per-360 (cm/360)

explanation.text: The number is a real distance. At 35 cm/360, moving the mouse 35 cm turns you all the way around in game.

citations.quote: For example, if your sensitivity is set at 35 cm/360, it means you will turn all the way around in game if you move your mouse 35 centimeters.

explanation.text: That only holds if the layers underneath are right. On controller output, your game settings must be set up correctly. The mouse DPI in your Config must also match your mouse.

citations.quote: Accurate real world velocity requires your game settings be configured correctly if outputting as controller, or, your velocity be calibrated correctly if outputting as mouse.
Accurate real world units require your mouse DPI be set correctly in your Config. Make sure this value matches your mouse DPI.

explanation.text: With Standard sync, you set the game's own sensitivity as XIM requires (normally its maximum). Your real aim speed is then set here, in the Config.

citations.quote: When a new Xbox Config is added to your XIM MATRIX, you may be reminded that you must set your game's in-game sensitivity to maximum (aim sensitivity is then customized in your Config).
When a new PC XInput Config is added to your XIM MATRIX, you may be reminded that you must set your game's in-game sensitivity to maximum (aim sensitivity is then customized in your Config).
Your aiming behavior is then set through your Config.

explanation.text: If your game has an ADS mode, Hip and ADS each have their own aim settings. By default ADS inherits everything from Hip. Choose "Sensitivity Only" to keep Hip's other settings but give ADS its own sensitivity.

citations.quote: If your game supports an Aim Down Sight mode, then, you'll be able to set both Hip and Aim Down Sight aiming independently. Otherwise, you'll have a single set of aim settings.
Inherit All: Inherit all ADS settings from Hip (this is the default)
Sensitivity Only: Inherit all ADS settings from Hip except sensitivity

explanation.text: cm/360 is defined for the default linear curve. A custom curve changes the real turn distance, and quantization may make it less accurate. When you check your sensitivity, use a linear curve and turn quantization off.

citations.quote: An accurate cm/360 means that your mouse behavior physically matches your sensitivity setting when using a linear (default) aim response curve.
Applying quantization to your mouse or motion aim may negatively affect real world sensitivity accuracy.
You are testing with a linear aiming curve (not a custom one)
You have quantization disabled

explanation.text: Motion (gyro) aim has its own sensitivity, measured in times-degrees-per-second instead of cm/360.

citations.quote: Motion (gyro) sensitivity is set in times-degrees-per-second
Mouse sensitivity is set in centimeters-per-360 (cm/360)

guidance.text: Start with Sensitivity alone. Change other values only if you need to. XIM says there is no "right" set of values: it's preference.

citations.quote: Always start with just adjusting Sensitivity. Change other values only if necessary. There is no "right" set of values. It is preference that matches your gaming style.

guidance.text: To check that your cm/360 is accurate, XIM's test is: set 40 cm/360, go somewhere without enemies (aim assist slows the reticle), then move the mouse 10 cm at moderate speed. You should turn a quarter turn (90 degrees). Use a linear curve and switch quantization off first. On Xbox with an Elite 2 controller, turn off its stick curve.

citations.quote: Set your mouse sensitivity to 40 cm/360
Start your game in a training area or private match (without enemies that can cause aim assist slowdown)
Move your mouse at a moderate speed horizontally 10 centimeters (which is a quarter turn, 90-degrees)
You are testing with a linear aiming curve (not a custom one)
You have quantization disabled
If using an Elite 2 on Xbox, make sure you don't have a controller stick curve enabled

guidance.text: Exact cm/360 isn't needed to enjoy the MATRIX. It matters if you want the same sensitivity across your Configs, or want to use Configs from others.

citations.quote: Although an accurate cm/360 isn't strictly necessary to be able to use and enjoy you XIM MATRIX, it is required if you want:
Consistent sensitivity between your Configs
To effectively share and use Configs from others

guidance.text: Only if you use Simulate Analog Behavior (SAB): don't go faster than 20 cm/360. Remember that higher cm/360 values are slower.

citations.quote: Make sure your mouse sensitivity isn't faster than 20 cm/360.
Remember that higher cm/360 values are slower.

guidance.caveat: Applies only when Simulate Analog Behavior (SAB) is on. SAB is a controller-output feature for games with extra input requirements.

aimStyles.text: All aim styles, in different directions. A lower cm/360 turns you further per centimeter, which helps big turns and snaps. A higher cm/360 gives more mouse travel per degree, which helps the small, careful corrections of tracking and precision holds. Where you land is personal.

citations.quote: Mouse sensitivity is in cm/360 or "distance (in centimeters) to perform a full turn". That means, lower values produce faster aiming speeds.
Always start with just adjusting Sensitivity. Change other values only if necessary. There is no "right" set of values. It is preference that matches your gaming style.

aimStyles.reasoning: cm/360 is the mouse distance for a full turn, and lower values are faster (official definition). More distance per degree means a small hand movement moves the reticle less; less distance means a big turn needs less hand movement. No source ties a sensitivity value to an aim style, and XIM says there is no "right" set of values.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: In-game look sensitivity
notToBeConfusedWith.note: The game's own sensitivity setting. With Standard sync it stays at the value XIM requires; you tune your aim speed with this MATRIX Sensitivity instead.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Thumbstick sensitivity
notToBeConfusedWith.note: Aim speed for a physical stick. Depending on the Config type, it is set in-game or as a percentage of the game's maximum turn speed, not in cm/360.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Modify Aim Sensitivity
notToBeConfusedWith.note: A Smart Action that changes sensitivity only while its binding runs (for example in vehicles). It doesn't change this base value.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Sight Modifiers
notToBeConfusedWith.note: Per-scope sensitivity changes, available with Custom Game Settings.

terms.name: Y Scale
terms.location: Mouse Aim or Motion Aim: press the "..." for additional options.
terms.summary: Changes vertical aim sensitivity only, so up-down speed can differ from left-right.

definition.text: Y Scale is "vertical only sensitivity". It sits with the Aiming Curve and Quantization under the "..." additional options.

citations.quote: Press the "..." for additional options like setting an Aiming Curve, adjusting Y Scale (vertical only sensitivity), and applying aim Quantization.
Press the "..." for additional options like setting an Aiming Curve, adjusting Y Scale (vertical only sensitivity), and applying aim Quantization.

explanation.text: It changes how fast the reticle moves up and down. Left-right speed stays as your Sensitivity sets it.

citations.quote: Press the "..." for additional options like setting an Aiming Curve, adjusting Y Scale (vertical only sensitivity), and applying aim Quantization.

explanation.text: The guide doesn't explain Y Scale's unit, range or default. Check what Manager shows before you change it.

guidance.text: XIM's advice for mouse aim: start with Sensitivity alone, and change other values, such as Y Scale, only if necessary.

citations.quote: Always start with just adjusting Sensitivity. Change other values only if necessary. There is no "right" set of values. It is preference that matches your gaming style.

aimStyles.text: Mostly tracking. Holding on a target through sustained fire means constant vertical correction against recoil. The guide links more vertical sensitivity to recoil control, though through a temporary Smart Action rather than Y Scale.

citations.quote: Press the "..." for additional options like setting an Aiming Curve, adjusting Y Scale (vertical only sensitivity), and applying aim Quantization.
If you prefer simply increasing your vertical aim sensitivity temporarily as a form of recoil control, you use can use a vertical only aim sensitivity modifier action.

aimStyles.reasoning: Y Scale is vertical-only sensitivity. The guide's "Vertical Sensitivity Boost" raises vertical sensitivity temporarily "as a form of recoil control", so vertical speed matters most where recoil does: sustained fire. No source recommends a Y Scale value for any aim style.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Vertical Sensitivity Boost
notToBeConfusedWith.note: A recoil technique in the guide: a Modify Aim Sensitivity action (Y Only) that raises vertical sensitivity only while its binding runs. Y Scale is a permanent Config setting.

terms.name: Smoothing
terms.location: Mouse Aim and Motion Aim, in your Config's aim settings.
terms.summary: Filters out noise from your hardware and your hand. Pick a preset, or tune Standard or Classic mode.

definition.text: Gaming input hardware and natural hand jitter can cause an noisy input environment. Smoothing solves this by providing additional stability and control to your aim.

citations.quote: Gaming input hardware and natural hand jitter can cause an noisy input environment. Smoothing solves this by providing additional stability and control to your aim.
XIM MATRIX includes an advanced aim smoothing system that enables the gamer to tune their aim response to their preference.

explanation.text: There are two modes. Standard adapts to how fast you are aiming. Classic applies fixed (static) smoothing. Press the smoothing button (it reads STANDARD or CLASSIC) to switch.

citations.quote: You can also customize the smoothing system and choose between two smoothing modes: Standard and Classic.
Press the the smoothing button (i.e. "STANDARD" or "CLASSIC") to change modes.
The Standard system provides dynamic smoothing behavior that adapts to your current aim speed.
The Classic system is based on our past generation XIM APEX device which provides static smoothing behavior. It has been upgraded to provide additional customization and flexibility.

explanation.text: Mouse aim and motion aim each have their own smoothing presets.

citations.quote: Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.

explanation.text: Hip and ADS can only have different smoothing with the "Inherit Nothing" option. "Inherit All" (the default) and "Sensitivity Only" both copy Hip's smoothing to ADS.

citations.quote: Inherit All: Inherit all ADS settings from Hip (this is the default)
Sensitivity Only: Inherit all ADS settings from Hip except sensitivity
Inherit Nothing: Inherit no ADS settings from Hip

explanation.reasoning: Inherit All copies all ADS settings from Hip; Sensitivity Only copies all of them except sensitivity; Inherit Nothing copies none. Smoothing is one of those other settings, so only Inherit Nothing leaves ADS smoothing free.

explanation.text: The guide doesn't list the smoothing presets' names or what values they use. Check what your Manager offers.

feel.text: What it's for: aim that looks noisy or shaky because of your hardware or natural hand jitter. Smoothing adds stability and control.

citations.quote: Gaming input hardware and natural hand jitter can cause an noisy input environment. Smoothing solves this by providing additional stability and control to your aim.

guidance.text: Start with the presets. Try each one and keep what feels most natural. XIM says it's strictly preference.

citations.quote: Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.

guidance.text: Only if you use Simulate Analog Behavior (SAB): keep smoothing on. Use a preset, or if you use custom values, don't go below the presets' smoothing intensity.

citations.quote: Make sure your mouse or motion aim smoothing is not disabled.
It's recommended you use one of the smoothing presets. If you are using "custom", ensure you do not reduce smoothing intensity below that of the presets.

guidance.caveat: Applies only when Simulate Analog Behavior (SAB) is on. SAB is a controller-output feature for games with extra input requirements.

aimStyles.text: Tracking most. Holding on a target is a long run of small movements, and small movements are where jitter shows. Snaps and precision holds need smoothing too, but the trade-offs sit in the individual settings (Precision, Response, Easing).

citations.quote: Gaming input hardware and natural hand jitter can cause an noisy input environment. Smoothing solves this by providing additional stability and control to your aim.
Increase to provide extra stability at rest due to hand jitter and instability (motion aim only).

aimStyles.reasoning: Smoothing's official purpose is countering hardware and hand jitter. The guide's Stability setting ties hand jitter to aim at rest (for motion aim), so jitter likely shows most when the reticle is still or moving slowly, which is most of tracking. No source ties smoothing to aim styles.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Smooth
notToBeConfusedWith.note: A single Classic-mode setting. The guide says it was "Known previously as Smoothing".

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Smooth ADS Transition
notToBeConfusedWith.note: An ADS Activation Delay option that blends the reticle's movement while switching to ADS. It is not aim smoothing.

terms.name: Standard
terms.location: Smoothing, in Mouse Aim or Motion Aim. Press the smoothing button to switch between STANDARD and CLASSIC.
terms.summary: The smoothing mode that adapts to your aim speed. Tuned with Precision, Response, Easing and Stability.

definition.text: The Standard system provides dynamic smoothing behavior that adapts to your current aim speed.

citations.quote: The Standard system provides dynamic smoothing behavior that adapts to your current aim speed.

explanation.text: It splits your aim by speed. Precision handles slow, fine aim. Response handles fast aim. Easing handles the start from rest. Stability handles holding still, for motion aim only.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Controls fast aim behavior
Specifies aim behavior from rest
Specifies aim behavior at rest
Increase to provide extra stability at rest due to hand jitter and instability (motion aim only).

guidance.text: Try the presets first. XIM says smoothing is strictly preference.

citations.quote: Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.

aimStyles.text: Dialed's weapon-aware advice assumes Standard. Because it adapts to aim speed, it can treat slow tracking and fast snaps differently within one Config. Classic applies the same smoothing at every speed.

citations.quote: The Standard system provides dynamic smoothing behavior that adapts to your current aim speed.
The Classic system is based on our past generation XIM APEX device which provides static smoothing behavior. It has been upgraded to provide additional customization and flexibility.
Controls fine aim behavior
Controls fast aim behavior

aimStyles.reasoning: Standard "adapts to your current aim speed" and has separate settings for fine and fast aim. Classic "provides static smoothing behavior". Only a speed-adaptive mode can favour slow and fast aim differently at the same time.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Standard (Game Settings sync)
notToBeConfusedWith.note: A sync method: in-game sensitivity at maximum, required settings applied, everything else default. Unrelated to smoothing.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Standard (Velocity Mapping)
notToBeConfusedWith.note: The default Velocity Mapping: your top speed maps to the game's maximum for each aiming angle. Unrelated to smoothing.

statement.text: The Config's update rate: how fast the MATRIX updates your console or PC. The guide's SAB checklist says to keep it at Standard, the default. Unrelated to Standard smoothing.

citations.quote: When configuring the output connection mode of your Config, you can choose how fast you want your XIM MATRIX to update your console. Keep this value at "Standard" (which is default).

terms.name: Precision
terms.location: Smoothing, Standard mode (Mouse Aim or Motion Aim).
terms.summary: Standard smoothing for slow, fine aim. Higher is smoother but heavier.

definition.text: Controls fine aim behavior. Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

explanation.text: It acts on slow movements: the small corrections you make while lining up or holding on a target. Raising it smooths those movements more.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

explanation.text: Lowering it should do the opposite: small adjustments feel lighter but get less smoothing.

citations.quote: Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

explanation.reasoning: The guide only describes raising it (smoother, heavier). Lowering it is the reverse of that stated trade-off.

explanation.text: The guide doesn't give this setting's range or default. Check what Manager shows before you change it.

feel.text: Higher Precision makes the reticle feel heavier at low speed, in return for a smoother result.

citations.quote: Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

citations.quote: Both mouse and motion have different presets designed for those aiming methods. Start by trying each out to see what feels most natural to you. It's strictly based on preference.

aimStyles.text: Tracking: the main lever. Raising Precision steadies your hold through sustained fire, at the cost of a heavier reticle. If small corrections feel sluggish, lower it.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

aimStyles.reasoning: Tracking is mostly slow, fine movement, which is what Precision controls ("fine aim behavior", "smoother result at low aim speeds"). The heaviness trade-off comes from the same definition.

aimStyles.text: Precision hold: matters too. Lining up one careful shot is slow, fine movement. More Precision gives a steadier line-up but a heavier feel.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior
Higher values provide a smoother result at low aim speeds and increases the heaviness of the reticle.

aimStyles.reasoning: Precision acts at low aim speeds, and a deliberate line-up happens at low speed.

aimStyles.text: Snap: matters less. A snap is mostly fast movement, which Response and Easing cover. Precision still shapes the small correction at the end of a snap.

citations.quote: Controls fine aim behavior

Specifies aim behavior from rest

aimStyles.reasoning: Precision is defined for fine aim at low speeds only. Fast aim and the start from rest belong to Response and Easing.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Micro (Advanced SAB)
notToBeConfusedWith.note: An Advanced SAB value that "Tunes stick behavior at very low aiming speeds". It belongs to Simulate Analog Behavior, not to smoothing.

explanation.text: Its settings are Sensitivity (in times-degrees-per-second) and Smoothing, plus the same extra options as mouse aim: Aiming Curve, Y Scale and Quantization.

citations.quote: Motion aim settings consists of Sensitivity and Smoothing.
Motion (gyro) sensitivity is set in times-degrees-per-second
Press the "..." for additional options like setting an Aiming Curve, adjusting Y Scale (vertical only sensitivity), and applying aim Quantization.

explanation.text: Stability, in Standard smoothing, applies to motion aim only.

citations.quote: Increase to provide extra stability at rest due to hand jitter and instability (motion aim only).

guidance.text: New to motion aim? Ease into it. Use motion for fine aim and the thumbstick for coarse aim. Start with a very low sensitivity and lean on the stick at first.

citations.quote: If you are new to motion aim, ease into it. Use motion for fine aim and thumbstick for coarse. Start with very low sensitivity and rely more on thumbstick aim initially.

guidance.text: Quick Pull with hair triggers adds stability when firing with motion aim, because you don't press and release the trigger fully.

citations.quote: Quick Pull with hair triggers also provides additional stability when firing using motion gyro aim. It reduces the physical force of the trigger by not requiring full press and release which can cause your gamepad to move.

aimStyles.text: Tracking and precision holds. XIM's tip for players new to motion aim is motion for fine aim and the stick for coarse aim, and fine aim is what those styles need. Snaps and big turns go to the stick.

citations.quote: If you are new to motion aim, ease into it. Use motion for fine aim and thumbstick for coarse. Start with very low sensitivity and rely more on thumbstick aim initially.

aimStyles.reasoning: XIM's tip for players new to motion aim: "Use motion for fine aim and thumbstick for coarse." Tracking and precision holds are mostly fine aim; snaps and big turns are coarse.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Engage, Pause and Toggle Motion Aim

statement.text: Smart Actions for motion aim, not motion aim settings. Engage and Pause work only while the action is active. Toggle switches motion aim on or off, and only works with the Custom Toggle activation mode.

citations.quote: Enable gyro motion aim. Only enabled while action is active. Use to customize motion enablement beyond the built in motion activation methods. Requires a supported gyro controller.
Pause gyro motion aim. Only pauses while action is active. Requires a supported gyro controller.
Toggles gyro motion aim on/off. Only works with the custom motion toggle activation method. Requires a supported gyro controller.

statement.text: The official XIM MATRIX guide lists no setting called Steady Aim. A XIM Central MATRIX-era video title uses the name for quantization, but we couldn't review that video, so Dialed can't say whether the two work the same way. For the MATRIX setting, see Quantization.

The official XIM MATRIX guide lists no setting called Boost. XIM Central has a MATRIX-era video about a "Boost Feature", but we couldn't review it, so Dialed says nothing about it yet. For the guide's "Vertical Sensitivity Boost", see Modify Aim Sensitivity.
